name: Algorithms
author: Recurse
subject: cs
description: Searching, sorting compared, recursion, divide and conquer, greedy vs dynamic programming, and BFS and DFS, in Python.

lesson.intro: An algorithm is a precise recipe that turns input into output. A handful of classics show up everywhere: in the libraries you call, in interviews and in fast code. This pack covers searching, sorting, recursion, divide and conquer, greedy choices, dynamic programming and graph search.
objectives: Define an algorithm and work a new problem from brute force to better
Implement binary search correctly and say when it beats linear search
Compare the classic sorts by time, space, stability and in-place behavior
Trace recursion, and tell when greedy works and when DP is needed
Choose BFS or DFS for a graph problem and justify the choice

sections.title: What an algorithm is
sections.key: An algorithm is a finite list of precise steps that turns input into output: correct for every valid input, always finishing, and efficient as input grows.
sections.body:
Before a map app shows your route, it runs a procedure guaranteed to find the fastest path. Before your inbox appears, a procedure sorts it by date. Each is an **algorithm**.

[[visual]]

"Precise" is the key word. "Add salt until it tastes right" works for a cook, but it gives a computer no exact rule, so two runs could differ and nothing says when to stop. "Add 5 grams" is a step.

In `find_max`, two decisions make it correct: it starts from the first item, not 0 (wrong for an all-negative list), and it refuses an empty list.

[[code]]

For any new problem, in an interview or at work:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Three properties of every algorithm
rows: right output for every valid input
an edge case: empty list, one item, duplicates, negatives
a loop that never ends, a recursion that never reaches its base case
time and memory stay reasonable as input grows (Big-O)
a slow approach on big input

steps.label: Work a small example by hand
Write a simple brute-force solution that is correct
Analyze its time and space cost
Find the bottleneck and apply a better idea
steps.detail: sort first, use a hash map, halve the search, reuse earlier results

steps.label: Test the final version on your examples and edge cases

sections.pitfall: Testing only the happy path. Most wrong algorithms fail on an edge case: empty input, one item, all items equal, negative numbers, or the answer at the very first or last position.

check.question: A max function starts with best = 0 and keeps any larger item it sees. For which input does it return a wrong answer?
check.explanation: No item in [-5, -2, -9] is larger than 0, so it returns 0, a number that is not even in the list. Starting from the first item fixes it.

sections.title: Searching: linear vs binary
sections.key: Linear search is O(n) on any list; binary search is O(log n) but needs sorted data, discarding half the remaining range with every probe.
sections.body:
Look up "nebula" in a paper dictionary: you open near the middle, see "mango", and know the word is in the second half. That is **binary search**, and it only works because the dictionary is sorted.

[[visual]]

Keep a range [lo, hi] that must hold the target if it exists. Probe the middle, then move lo past mid or hi before mid:

[[visual 2]]

Loop while `lo <= hi` (with `lo < hi`, a one-item range is never checked) and always move past mid, or the range can stop shrinking.

[[code]]

Sorted data also unlocks **two pointers**: for a pair with a given sum, start at both ends; move the left one right if the sum is too small, the right one left if too big. That is O(n), not O(n^2).

visual.title: Worst-case comparisons
visual.caption: Binary search needs about log2(n) + 1 probes. One search on unsorted data? Scan it: sorting first costs O(n log n), more than one O(n) scan.

visual.title: Searching for 16
visual.caption: 12 < 16, so go right. 23 > 16, so go left. Now lo, mid and hi all sit at index 4: found in 3 probes.

sections.code:
def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:        # range not empty
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1   # target is right
        else:
            hi = mid - 1   # target is left
    return -1              # not present

nums = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56]
print(binary_search(nums, 16))   # 4
print(binary_search(nums, 7))    # -1
sections.tip: In production Python, use `bisect.bisect_left(nums, x)`: it returns the index of x, or the index where x would be inserted to keep the list sorted.
sections.pitfall: Running binary search on unsorted data. It does not crash; it quietly returns wrong answers, because discarding half the range is only safe when the order proves the target is not there.

activity.title: Halve the range
activity.prompt: Choose every probe yourself. Pick the exact middle of the remaining range each time and you will always finish within the probe limit; pick off-center once and see how much less that probe rules out. After each find, compare your probe count with the linear scan count.

check.question: Binary search runs on a sorted list of 1,000 items. About how many probes does it need in the worst case?
check.explanation: Each probe halves the range, and 2^10 = 1,024, so about 10 halvings shrink 1,000 items to one. About 500 is the average for a linear scan that finds its target.

sections.title: Simple sorts: bubble, selection, insertion
sections.key: Bubble, selection and insertion sort are all O(n^2) and in place; insertion sort is near O(n) on nearly sorted data, and selection sort is not stable.
sections.body:
Sorting a hand of cards, you slide each new card into place among those you hold. That is **insertion sort**. The simple sorts show the core moves (compare, swap, shift), and interviewers ask about them.

[[visual]]

A **stable** sort keeps items with equal keys in their original order. Sort a spreadsheet by last name and people who share a last name stay in their earlier order. Selection sort's long-distance swap can jump an item over an equal one, so it is not stable.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

rows: swap out-of-order neighbors; after pass k the last k items are final; stop early after a pass with no swaps
O(n^2); O(n) on sorted input with the early exit
swap the smallest unsorted item to the front, repeat
always n(n - 1)/2, even on sorted input; at most n - 1 swaps
shift each new item left past larger ones into a sorted prefix
O(n^2) worst; close to O(n) on nearly sorted data
visual.caption: All three sort in place with O(1) extra memory. Library sorts use insertion sort on small or nearly sorted chunks.

visual.title: Bubble sort, first pass
visual.caption: 4 swaps with 2; then 5 bubbles past 1 and 3. The largest item, 5, is now final.

visual.title: Insertion sort: the sorted prefix grows

sections.code:
def insertion_sort(items):
    for i in range(1, len(items)):
        current = items[i]
        j = i - 1
        # shift larger items one place right
        while j >= 0 and items[j] > current:
            items[j + 1] = items[j]
            j -= 1
        items[j + 1] = current  # fill gap
    return items

print(insertion_sort([5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]))
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
sections.pitfall: Calling insertion sort always slow. O(n^2) is its worst case; on nearly sorted data it is close to O(n), which is exactly why real sorting libraries use it on small runs.

activity.title: Three simple sorts
activity.prompt: Predict which of the three needs the fewest comparisons, then run all three on the same array. Now switch the starting shape to Nearly sorted and run them again: insertion sort's count collapses, while selection sort's stays exactly the same.

check.question: Which simple sort makes the same number of comparisons however the input is arranged?
choices: Bubble sort with an early exit
None of them: all three adapt to the input
check.explanation: Selection sort always scans the whole unsorted part to find its minimum: n(n - 1)/2 comparisons on any input. Insertion sort and bubble sort with an early exit both finish fast on sorted input.

sections.title: Recursion
sections.key: A recursive function needs a base case that answers directly and a recursive case on a smaller input; every call still waiting holds a stack frame.
sections.body:
To count nesting dolls, open the outer one, count it, then count the dolls inside: the same problem, only smaller. That is **recursion**.

- **Base case**: answers directly, without recursing. It stops the descent.
- **Recursive case**: calls the function on a smaller input and uses (returns) the result. Each call must move toward the base case.

[[code]]

Each call gets a **stack frame** with its arguments and locals. Frames pile up on the **call stack** until a base case returns, then unwind:

[[visual]]

So recursion uses O(depth) memory, and Python raises RecursionError past about 1,000 nested calls. Any recursion can be rewritten as a loop with an explicit stack.

Naive Fibonacci re-solves the same subproblems: fib(30) makes about 2.7 million calls. **Memoization** stores each result, so each of the 31 values is computed once.

visual.title: The call stack for factorial(5)
visual.arrowLabel: Calls pile up to the base case, then each waiting call finishes

sections.deeper: Recursion fits self-similar problems: a tree is a node plus smaller trees, a folder holds smaller folders, JSON nests objects in objects, and divide and conquer splits input into halves that are solved the same way. For very deep inputs (a linked list of a million nodes), rewrite it as a loop with an explicit stack, because the call stack is far smaller than the heap.
sections.tip: Return the recursive call's result. Writing `count_down(n - 1)` instead of `return count_down(n - 1)` throws the answer away, and the function returns None.
sections.pitfall: A base case the input can skip past. `if n == 0` never fires when n starts odd and drops by 2 each call. Prefer `if n <= 0`, and check that every call moves toward the base case.

activity.title: Calls and the call stack
activity.prompt: Run fib(6) without memoization and count the calls; notice how many times fib(2) is computed. Then switch memoization on and run it again. Keep an eye on the call stack panel: its height, not the total number of calls, is the memory the recursion needs.

check.question: What limits how deep recursion can go in Python?
choices: The number of CPU cores in the machine
Nothing: recursion depth is unlimited in Python
The size of the heap, because every call copies its arguments
The call stack: each pending call holds a frame, and Python stops at a recursion limit (1,000 by default)
check.explanation: Every call that has not returned yet keeps a stack frame. Python caps the depth (sys.getrecursionlimit() is 1,000 by default) and raises RecursionError past it, long before the machine would run out of memory.

sections.title: Divide and conquer: merge sort and quicksort
sections.key: Divide and conquer splits a problem, solves the parts recursively and combines them: merge sort always halves and merges, quicksort partitions around a pivot.
sections.body:
Sorting 1,000 exam papers alone is slow. Split the pile, hand halves to friends who split again, then merge the sorted piles back. That is **divide and conquer**.

**Merge sort** splits by position, so it always makes about log2(n) levels, and each level merges n items in O(n):

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

**Quicksort** picks a **pivot** and **partitions**: smaller items to its left, the rest to its right. The pivot is now final, each side is sorted recursively, and no merge is needed.

[[visual 3]]

Binary search is divide and conquer that keeps only one half.

steps.label: Does the list have 0 or 1 items?
Split the list into two halves
Merge the sorted halves
steps.detail: repeatedly take the smaller front item

visual.title: Merge sort splits, then merges back up

items.title: Merge sort
points: O(n log n) in every case: the splits ignore the data
Stable if the merge takes from the left half on ties
O(n) extra memory for the merged output

items.title: Quicksort
points: O(n log n) on average, in place, cache friendly, fast in practice
O(n^2) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest, as with the last item of a sorted list
Random or median-of-three pivots make that very unlikely
Not stable; O(log n) stack on average

sections.deeper: Why does a bad pivot cost O(n^2)? If the pivot is always the smallest or largest item, each partition peels off just one item, so the levels hold n, n - 1, n - 2, ... 1 items and the total is about n^2/2. The same split, solve, combine pattern powers fast multiplication algorithms and many tree algorithms.
sections.pitfall: Calling quicksort O(n log n) without saying which case. That is its average; its worst case is O(n^2). Say so, and add that random pivots make the worst case vanishingly rare.

activity.title: Merge sort vs quicksort
activity.prompt: Run merge sort and quicksort on the same random array and compare their comparison counts with insertion sort. Then load the Reversed shape and run quicksort again. This quicksort uses the last item as its pivot, so watch how lopsided the partitions become and how the count jumps.

check.question: Why is merge sort O(n log n) even on its worst input?
choices: It skips items that are already in order
It always halves the list, giving about log2(n) levels, and merging costs O(n) per level
It picks a random pivot, so bad splits are rare
It only ever compares neighboring items
check.explanation: The splits do not depend on the data, so the recursion is always about log2(n) levels deep, and each level does O(n) merging work. A random pivot is quicksort's trick, not merge sort's.

sections.title: Sorting compared, and sorting in practice
sections.key: In real code you call the built-in sort (Python's Timsort is stable and O(n log n)); what you need is the trade-offs between sorts.
sections.body:
You almost never write a sort: you call `sorted()` or `list.sort()` in Python, or `array.sort()` in JavaScript. **In place** means O(1) extra memory beyond the input; **stable** means equal keys keep their order.

[[visual]]

Python's **Timsort** is a merge and insertion sort hybrid: O(n log n) worst, near O(n) on partly sorted data, and stable. Java uses it for objects, and JavaScript's sort must be stable since ES2019.

Stability makes multi-key sorting easy: sort by the secondary key first, then by the primary key with a stable sort.

[[code]]

No comparison sort beats O(n log n) in the worst case; that is a proven lower bound. Counting sort and radix sort go faster only by exploiting the keys, such as small integers in a known range.

visual.title: Sorting compared
visual.caption: Bubble sort's O(n) best case assumes the early exit. Quicksort's O(log n) is its recursion stack.

sections.code:
# By customer, then by date within each:
orders.sort(key=lambda o: o.date)
orders.sort(key=lambda o: o.customer)

# Or in one call with a tuple key:
orders.sort(
    key=lambda o: (o.customer, o.date))

nums = nums.sort()   # bug: returns None
nums = sorted(nums)  # returns a new list
sections.tip: To sort by several keys in one call, return a tuple from the key function. To reverse just one numeric key, negate it: `key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.name)`.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting the comparator in JavaScript. The default sort compares items as strings, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 9]`. For numbers, write `nums.sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

check.question: You must sort 10 million records, memory is tight, and stability does not matter. Which is the most reasonable choice?
check.explanation: Quicksort sorts in place and runs in O(n log n) on average, and random pivots make the O(n^2) case vanishingly unlikely. Merge sort needs O(n) extra memory, and the O(n^2) simple sorts would need around 10^14 steps.

sections.title: Greedy algorithms and dynamic programming
sections.key: Greedy takes the best-looking step and never reconsiders, which can be wrong; dynamic programming solves each overlapping subproblem once and tries every option.
sections.body:
A cashier making 63 cents in US coins grabs the biggest coin that fits: 25, 25, 10, 1, 1, 1. Six coins, the fewest possible. That is a **greedy algorithm**. With coins 1, 6 and 10, though, greedy makes 12 as 10 + 1 + 1, while 6 + 6 needs two.

[[visual]]

**Dynamic programming (DP)** applies when a problem has both:

- **Optimal substructure**: the best answer is built from best answers to smaller subproblems.
- **Overlapping subproblems**: the same smaller subproblems keep coming up, as fib(3) does inside fib(6).

**Top-down** DP is recursion plus memoization. **Bottom-up** DP fills a table from the smallest subproblem up:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

items.title: Greedy
points: Takes the locally best choice and never reconsiders
Simple and fast
Provably optimal for some problems: most meetings in a room (earliest end first), Dijkstra, Huffman codes
Break it with a small counterexample before trusting it

items.title: Dynamic programming
points: Considers every option for each subproblem
Stores each result so it is solved once
Optimal when the two properties hold
Coin change costs O(amount × number of coins)

visual.title: Bottom-up: fewest coins for 12 with coins 1, 6, 10

steps.label: best[a] is the fewest coins that make a
Fill amounts 1 to 11 the same way
For 12, try every coin c: 1 + best[12 - c]
steps.work:
coin 1:  1 + best[11] = 3
coin 6:  1 + best[6] = 2
coin 10: 1 + best[2] = 3

sections.code:
def greedy_coins(coins, amount):
    count = 0
    # biggest coin first
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):
        count += amount // c
        amount %= c
    return count

def dp_coins(coins, amount):
    best = [0] + [float("inf")] * amount
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        options = [best[a - c] + 1
                   for c in coins if c <= a]
        best[a] = min(options + [best[a]])
    return best[amount]

print(greedy_coins([1, 6, 10], 12))  # 3
print(dp_coins([1, 6, 10], 12))      # 2
sections.deeper: A rule of thumb: try greedy when a simple local rule seems right, then either prove it or break it with a counterexample. When choices interact and you keep re-solving the same smaller question, reach for DP. The swe-dynamic-programming pack goes much deeper, including how to define the state and the recurrence.
sections.pitfall: Trusting a greedy rule because it worked on your first example. Greedy change-making is optimal for US coins but not for 1, 6 and 10. Hunt for a counterexample before you commit.

check.question: Coins are 1, 3 and 4. For an amount of 6, what does the greedy rule (largest coin first) do, and what is optimal?
choices: Greedy uses 2 coins (3 + 3), which is optimal
Greedy uses 6 coins (six 1s); the optimum is 2
Greedy uses 3 coins (4 + 1 + 1); the optimum is 2 (3 + 3)
check.explanation: Greedy grabs the 4 first and is left with 2, which needs two 1s. It never reconsiders the 4, so it misses 3 + 3. DP would try every coin at every amount and find the 2-coin answer.

sections.title: Graph search: BFS and DFS
sections.key: BFS explores in layers with a queue and finds fewest-edge paths; DFS goes deep with a stack or recursion; both need a visited set and cost O(V + E).
sections.body:
Lost in a maze, you can check every square one step away, then two steps, like ripples: the first ripple to reach the exit traced the shortest route. Or follow one corridor to its end and back up at dead ends. The first is **breadth-first search (BFS)**, the second **depth-first search (DFS)**.

[[visual]]

Both need a **visited** set, because graphs have cycles. The difference is which waiting vertex goes next:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

For weighted graphs, fewest edges is not cheapest: **Dijkstra's algorithm** swaps the queue for a priority queue.

visual.title: The graph, with BFS distances from A

items.title: BFS
points: Explores in layers by distance from the start
First reach of a vertex uses the fewest edges
Shortest paths in unweighted graphs, minimum-moves puzzles, degrees of separation

items.title: DFS
items.sub: a stack or recursion: newest first
points: Goes deep before wide: A, B, D, C, E, F here
Explore everything reachable, detect cycles, count components
Backtracking and topological sort

visual.caption: Both are O(V + E) with an adjacency list: each vertex visited once, each edge examined once (twice if undirected).

visual.title: The BFS queue from A
visual.caption: Each vertex is marked visited when it is queued, so D joins only once.

sections.pitfall: Marking vertices visited too late. If BFS marks a vertex only when it leaves the queue, several neighbors can queue it first; if DFS skips the visited check, it loops around a cycle until it crashes.

activity.title: BFS vs DFS on a maze
activity.prompt: Load a maze and run BFS, then DFS, from the same start. Compare their path lengths and how many cells each visited: BFS's path is always the shortest, while DFS often finds a long, winding one. Then draw a wall across the short route and predict BFS's new answer before you run it.

check.question: What single change makes the BFS above explore depth-first instead?
choices: Sort each neighbor list before the loop
Replace popleft() with pop(), so the newest vertex is explored next
check.explanation: Taking from the same end you add to turns the queue into a stack, so the most recently discovered vertex is explored first: depth-first order. Removing the visited check would only make it loop on cycles.

keyTerms.definition: A finite sequence of precise steps that turns an input into the desired output, correctly and in finite time.
Searching sorted data by repeatedly checking the middle of the remaining range and discarding the half that cannot hold the target. O(log n).
A sort that keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order. Merge sort, insertion sort and Timsort are stable.
Using only O(1) extra memory beyond the input, apart from a small recursion stack.
The input a recursive function answers directly, without recursing, which stops the recursion.
Splitting a problem into smaller copies of itself, solving them recursively, and combining the answers.
The item quicksort partitions around: smaller items go to its left, the rest to its right.
An algorithm that takes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it. Fast, but correct only for some problems.
Solving a problem by storing and reusing answers to overlapping subproblems, top-down with memoization or bottom-up with a table.
Caching each function result the first time it is computed so repeated calls return instantly.
Breadth-first search: explore a graph layer by layer with a queue. Finds fewest-edge paths in unweighted graphs.
Depth-first search: follow one path as deep as possible before backing up, using a stack or recursion.

summary: An algorithm must be correct for every valid input, terminate, and stay efficient.
Linear search is O(n) on any list; binary search is O(log n) on sorted data.
Simple sorts are O(n^2); merge sort is always O(n log n) and stable; quicksort is in place but O(n^2) with bad pivots.
Recursion needs a base case and a smaller call; each pending call holds a stack frame.
Greedy can be wrong; dynamic programming stores overlapping subproblems and tries every option.
BFS (queue) finds fewest-edge paths, DFS (stack) goes deep; both are O(V + E).
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how you would find a word in a 1,000-page dictionary, why that only works because the dictionary is sorted, and how the same 'split the job in half' idea lets merge sort sort a huge pile of papers quickly.

questions.question: What must be true of a list before binary search can be used on it?
choices: Its length is a power of two
questions.explanation: Binary search decides which half to discard by comparing with the middle item, which only works if smaller items are on one side and larger ones on the other. Duplicates and any length are fine, and it works on any comparable items, such as strings.

questions.question: binary_search([2, 4, 6], 6) returns -1 even though 6 is in the list. What is the bug?
choices: The loop should run while lo <= hi; with lo < hi it never checks a one-item range
mid should be computed as (lo + hi) / 2
lo = mid + 1 should be lo = mid
The comparison items[mid] < target should use >
questions.explanation: After the first step lo and hi are both 2: a one-item range that holds 6. lo < hi is False, so the loop exits without looking at it. Using / gives a float that cannot index a list, and lo = mid can loop forever because the range stops shrinking.

questions.question: Fill the blank to complete this two-pointer palindrome check.
questions.explanation: After a matching pair, both pointers move inward: left goes right and right goes left, until they meet. right += 1 would move past the end of the string and raise IndexError.

questions.question: Two pointers moving inward from both ends find a pair with a given sum in a sorted list of n items. What is the worst-case time complexity? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Each step moves one pointer one place inward, and the scan stops when the pointers meet, so there are at most n - 1 steps. Checking every pair with nested loops would be O(n^2).

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: Starting at 5 and subtracting 2 gives 3, 1, -1, -3 and so on: n is never exactly 0, so the base case is skipped and the calls never stop. 9 is what you would get if the recursion stopped at 1. A safer base case is `if n <= 0`.

questions.question: This prints None instead of "done". Why?
choices: The base case should be n == 1
The recursive call's result is thrown away; it should be return count_down(n - 1)
questions.explanation: The base case does return "done", but only to the call one level up, which ignores it and falls off the end of the function, returning None. Every level must pass the result back with return.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: power(2, 5) is 2 * power(2, 4), which unfolds to 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * power(2, 0). The base case returns 1, so the result is 32.

questions.question: You sort a list of orders by date, then sort that result by customer with a stable sort. How are each customer's orders arranged?
questions.explanation: A stable sort keeps items with equal keys (the same customer) in the order they had going in, and going in they were sorted by date. This is how you sort by several keys with Python's sorted: sort by the minor key first, then by the major key.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: If every pivot is the smallest or largest item, as when the first item is the pivot of an already sorted list, each partition removes only one item: n + (n - 1) + ... + 1 steps. The average case is O(n log n), and random pivots make the worst case very unlikely.

questions.question: You need a sort that is guaranteed O(n log n) and stable, and extra memory is not a concern. Which fits?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is O(n log n) in every case and keeps equal items in order. Heap sort is also guaranteed O(n log n) but is not stable. Quicksort can hit O(n^2), and insertion sort is O(n^2) in the worst case.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the list ends up in ascending order and the sort stays stable.
questions.explanation: Larger items shift right to make room. Using > stops at an equal item, so equal items keep their original order. >= still sorts, but it moves the new item ahead of equal ones, which breaks stability. < would sort in descending order.

questions.question: Which structure decides the order in which BFS visits nodes?
questions.explanation: BFS takes nodes from the front of a queue and adds new neighbors to the back, so nodes are processed in the order they were discovered, layer by layer. Swapping the queue for a stack turns it into a depth-first search. The set only tracks which nodes have been seen.

questions.question: Called as bfs("A"), this never returns. What is wrong?
choices: It never records visited nodes, so the cycle A, B, C, A keeps refilling the queue
BFS cannot run on directed graphs
order.append(node) should come after the for loop
questions.explanation: The graph has a cycle, and without a visited set every node is queued again each time it is reached. Adding a visited set and skipping nodes already in it fixes this. Changing popleft to pop turns it into a depth-first search, but it would still loop forever.

questions.question: With an adjacency list, what is the time complexity of BFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges? Answer in Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: Each vertex is added to the queue and removed once, which is O(V), and each vertex's neighbor list is scanned once, which adds up to O(E) across the whole graph. DFS has the same cost.

questions.question: With coins of 1, 6 and 10, what does the greedy rule 'always take the largest coin that fits' do for an amount of 12?
choices: Fails, because 12 is not a multiple of 10
questions.explanation: Greedy takes 10 first and never reconsiders, leaving 2, which needs two 1s. It cannot see that skipping the 10 leads to a better total. Dynamic programming tries every coin for each amount and finds 6 + 6.

questions.question: Fill the blank to complete this memoized Fibonacci.
questions.explanation: If n is already cached, return the stored value instead of recomputing it. return fib(n) would call itself with the same n until RecursionError, and return memo would return the whole dict.

questions.question: What is the difference between a greedy algorithm and dynamic programming?
questions.answer: A greedy algorithm commits to the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it. Dynamic programming considers every option for each subproblem, stores each result, and builds the best overall answer from them.
questions.explanation: Greedy is faster and simpler but only correct for some problems; DP does more work but is correct whenever the problem breaks into overlapping subproblems.

questions.question: A recipe step says "add salt until it tastes right". Why would a step like that be a problem in an algorithm?
choices: It would run too slowly on a computer
It is not precise, so two runs could do different things and there is no exact rule for when to stop
Algorithms are not allowed to contain loops
It does not use any data structure
questions.explanation: Every step of an algorithm must be unambiguous, and the whole procedure must terminate. 'Until it tastes right' has no exact stopping rule. Loops are fine, as long as their condition is precise.

questions.question: Put these steps for tackling a new algorithm problem in a sensible order.
items: Work a small example by hand, including edge cases
Write a simple brute-force solution that is correct
Analyze its time and space cost
Find the bottleneck and apply a better idea
Test the final version against your examples and edge cases
questions.explanation: Understanding comes before code, and a correct slow solution gives you a baseline to analyze and improve. Testing at the end catches mistakes introduced while optimizing. Interviewers want to see exactly this progression.

questions.question: Binary search runs on a sorted list of 1,000,000 items. Roughly how many probes does it need in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Each probe halves the range, and 2^20 is about 1,048,576, so about 20 halvings shrink a million items to one. A linear search could need all 1,000,000 comparisons.

questions.question: You need to check once whether a value appears in an unsorted list of n items. Should you sort the list first so you can use binary search?
choices: Yes: binary search is O(log n), so the total is O(log n)
Yes: sorting makes every operation on the list faster
It makes no difference: both approaches are O(n)
No: sorting costs O(n log n), more than one O(n) linear scan
questions.explanation: Sorting costs O(n log n) before the first probe, which is more than the O(n) linear scan it replaces. Sorting pays off when you will search the same data many times.

questions.question: bisect_left returns the index of x, or the index where x would be inserted to keep the list sorted. Fill the blank so contains is correct for every input.
questions.code:
import bisect

def contains(nums, x):          # nums is sorted
    i = bisect.bisect_left(nums, x)
    return _____
questions.explanation: If x is larger than everything, bisect_left returns len(nums), so nums[i] alone would raise IndexError: the bounds check must come first. If x is missing, i points at the next larger item, so the equality check is needed too. bisect never returns -1.

questions.question: Which simple sort is fastest on a list that is already almost sorted?
choices: Bubble sort without an early exit
They are equally fast, since all are O(n^2)
questions.explanation: Insertion sort shifts each item only as far as it is out of place, so nearly sorted input costs close to O(n). Selection sort scans the entire unsorted part on every pass, whatever the input looks like.

questions.question: Selection sort runs on a list of 5 items. How many comparisons does it make?
questions.explanation: Finding the minimum of 5 items takes 4 comparisons, then 3 for the remaining 4, then 2, then 1: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, which is n(n - 1)/2. It makes the same 10 comparisons even when the list is already sorted.

questions.question: What does [5, 1, 4, 2, 8] look like after the first pass of bubble sort?
questions.explanation: The pass compares neighbors left to right: swap 5 and 1, swap 5 and 4, swap 5 and 2, then leave 5 and 8 alone. The 5 bubbles right until it meets 8. The list is not sorted yet, because 4 and 2 still need another pass.

questions.question: What are the two parts every recursive function needs, and what does each do?
questions.answer: A base case, which returns an answer directly without recursing and so stops the recursion, and a recursive case, which calls the function on a smaller input that moves toward the base case and uses the result.
questions.explanation: Without a reachable base case the calls never stop and Python raises RecursionError. Without a smaller input, each call just repeats the same problem.

questions.question: Match each sorting algorithm with its description.

pairs.right: O(n log n) in every case, stable, O(n) extra memory
O(n log n) on average, O(n^2) worst case, in place, not stable
O(n^2) worst case, close to O(n) on nearly sorted data, stable
Always n(n - 1)/2 comparisons, at most n - 1 swaps, not stable
Python's built-in sort: a stable merge and insertion sort hybrid

questions.explanation: These are the facts interviewers ask about most. Among the classic sorts, only merge sort guarantees O(n log n) and stability together, and Timsort builds on it.

questions.question: Put the steps of merge sort in order.
items: If the list has 0 or 1 items, return it as it is
Split the list into two halves
Merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item
questions.explanation: The base case comes first so the recursion can stop. The real work happens in the merge, which costs O(n) at each of the about log2(n) levels.

questions.question: A quicksort always uses the last item as its pivot. Which input makes it slowest?
choices: A list where every item is different
A list that is already sorted
questions.explanation: On sorted input the last item is the largest, so every partition puts everything on one side and removes only the pivot: n + (n - 1) + ... + 1 comparisons, O(n^2). Random input usually splits evenly. Choosing a random pivot fixes the sorted-input problem.

questions.question: Which pair of properties tells you dynamic programming will help?
choices: The input is sorted and has no duplicates
The input is a graph with no cycles
A greedy rule exists and always works
questions.explanation: DP builds the answer from best answers to smaller subproblems (optimal substructure) and saves time by solving each repeated subproblem only once (overlapping subproblems). If a greedy rule always works, you do not need DP at all.

questions.question: In an unweighted graph, which search finds a path with the fewest edges from the start to a target?
choices: Either one: both always return the shortest path
Neither: you must try every possible path
questions.explanation: BFS explores vertices in order of distance from the start, so the first time it reaches the target is along a fewest-edge path. DFS finds a path, but often a long, winding one.

questions.question: What does this code print? Type the letters separated by spaces.
questions.explanation: DFS follows the first unvisited neighbor as deep as it goes: A to B to D, a dead end. Only then does it return to A's next neighbor, C, and go on to E. BFS on the same graph would print A B C D E, layer by layer.

questions.question: A cashier uses the greedy rule (largest coin that fits) with US coins of 25, 10, 5 and 1 cents. How many coins does it hand out for 63 cents?
questions.explanation: 25 + 25 leaves 13, a 10 leaves 3, then three 1-cent coins: 6 coins in total. Greedy is always optimal for the US coin system, but for other coin sets, such as 1, 6 and 10, it can fail.
